newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish markets steady as convergence talk fades.
newsitem.headline: Finnish markets steady as convergence talk fades.

text.p: The Finnish markka had a stable first week safely parked in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), but bonds eased as analysts said the peg has left only scant short-term upward potential for the sector.
After Finland's ERM entry last weekend, a deceptive calm descended on financial markets which had risen on anticipation that the country would be among the first to join EMU in 1999.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin's dismissal of security chief Alexander Lebed on Thursday also unnerved the markets, depressing the markka and pushing bond yields higher.
The markka was steady at 2.99 per mark on Friday, exactly level with a week earlier when it was still floating freely.

It had been expected to strengthen further under buying pressure from exporters looking to repatriate earnings, but dealers said it had been held back by discreet intervention from the Bank of Finland to keep it relatively near its central parity rate in the ERM -- 3.04 per German mark.

Dealers said the Bank was a seller of markka at around 2.9850 per mark, but a central bank dealer as usual declined any comment. Traders were still guessing what kind of strategy the bank would adopt in the new currency regime.

The bank has said there is no secret band in which the markka should trade, besides the official 15 percent ERM fluctuation band, but dealers have guessed it would take action if the markka moves around 2.5-5 percent from the central rate.
"The peg removed the incentives to invest in markka ... there is no longer scope for much capital gains," said Pertti Thornberg, market advisor at Swedish bank Enskilda in Helsinki.

The yield spread between Finland's 2006 benchmark and its German equivalent, which shrank to about 40 basis points on Monday, was steady until the Russian uncertainty and looked set to end around 48 basis points, little changed on last Friday.

Bonds failed to react even when central bank governor Sirkka Hamalainen said earlier this week the German repo rate was no floor for the Finnish key rate, the money market tender rate, currently level with the repo at three percent.

Finnish bond portfolios have risen by over 15 percent this year as confidence increased that Finland would be among the first countries to qualify for a single currency, which is now almost fully priced into bonds, analysts said.
"I think the potential is much bigger in Sweden now," said Enskilda's Thornberg.
The Swedish nine-year bond on Friday yielded almost 80 basis points more than Finnish 2006 paper and analysts see little scope for Finland to narrow further over Germany near-term.
"In the near term I would say that everything below 40 basis points (on the 2006 bond) is a sell signal," said Teijo Rantatupa, treasury economist at OKOBANK.
If the single currency project stays on track this could narrow to some 25 to 35 basis points next year, he said.
Stocks passed a quiet monday but then sprang to life when an international rally carried them to new year-highs. Merita bank and telecoms major Nokia both rallied strongly.
The HEX on Friday climbed to its highest level since autumn 1995 to 2,259.69, dipping slightly as the weekend neared.
